senses.en: a machine, tool or idea that somebody has made for the first time
examples: The light bulb was one of the most useful **inventions** of the 19th century.
My little brother showed us his own **invention**: a robot made of paper cups.
Which **invention** has changed your daily life the most?

senses.en: the act of making something that did not exist before
senses.vi: việc sáng chế, sự phát minh
examples: The **invention** of the smartphone changed how we talk to each other.
Life became much faster after the **invention** of the aeroplane.

forms.en: a person who makes something new
forms.ex: Thomas Edison was a famous American **inventor**.

forms.en: good at thinking of new ideas
forms.vi: sáng tạo, giàu óc sáng chế
forms.ex: She is very **inventive** and always finds a clever solution.

invention.note: Use *the* **invention of** + noun when you mean the moment something was first made: *the invention of the printing press*.

senses.en: to make or design something completely new for the first time
examples: Who **invented** the telephone?
Students at our school **invented** a bag that charges a phone using sunlight.
Engineers are trying to **invent** a cheaper way to clean sea water.

forms.en: something new that has been made
forms.ex: The wheel is a very old **invention**.

forms.en: a person who invents things
forms.ex: The **inventor** received a prize for her design.

invent.note: **Invent** = create something that never existed (*Bell invented the telephone*). *Discover* = find something that was already there (*Scientists discovered a new planet*). This is a very common learner mistake.

senses.en: the use of body features such as fingerprints, faces or eyes to check who a person is
examples: **Biometrics** is now used at most international airports.
Our new phone uses **biometrics** instead of a password.
**Biometrics** makes it harder for someone to steal your identity.

forms.en: connected with measuring features of the human body
forms.ex: The school gate has a **biometric** scanner.

biometrics.note: **Biometrics** ends in *-s* but takes a **singular** verb: *Biometrics **is** used in banks.* (like *physics*, *economics*). Before a noun, use the adjective **biometric**: *a biometric passport*.

senses.en: the mark made by the lines on the end of your finger, which is different for every person
examples: I unlock my laptop with my **fingerprint**.
The police found a **fingerprint** on the glass.
No two people in the world have the same **fingerprints**.

fingerprint.note: Written as one word. The machine that reads it is a **fingerprint scanner** or **fingerprint reader**.

senses.en: the coloured ring around the black centre of your eye
examples: The camera scans your **iris** before the door opens.
Her **irises** are a very dark brown.
**Iris** recognition is faster than typing a password.

senses.en: a tall garden flower with long thin leaves, usually purple, blue or yellow
examples: My grandmother grows purple **irises** beside the pond.
There were yellow **irises** all along the river.

iris.note: Plural: **irises**. In technology texts you will almost always meet the eye meaning, as in *iris scanning*.

senses.en: the act of knowing who or what somebody or something is, especially by a machine
senses.vi: sự nhận dạng, sự nhận diện
examples: Face **recognition** lets you pay without a card.
Voice **recognition** software can type what you say.
**Recognition** of your fingerprint takes less than a second.

senses.en: public praise for what somebody has done well
senses.vi: sự công nhận, sự ghi nhận
examples: The young scientist finally got the **recognition** she deserved.
He received a medal in **recognition** of his work on clean energy.

forms.en: to know somebody or something because you have seen it before
forms.ex: The app **recognises** my face even in the dark.

recognition.note: British spelling **recognise**; American spelling *recognize*. Both are pronounced the same.

senses.en: a piece of equipment made to do a particular job
examples: This small **device** measures the air quality in the room.
You can log in on up to three **devices**.
Please switch off all electronic **devices** during the test.

device.note: **Device** is countable: *a device*, *two devices*. Use *equipment* (uncountable) for the general idea: *lab equipment*, not ~~lab equipments~~.

senses.en: the ability of computers to do things that normally need human thinking, such as learning and making decisions
examples: **Artificial intelligence** can translate a whole book in seconds.
Doctors use **artificial intelligence** to read X-ray pictures.
Our teacher explained how **artificial intelligence** learns from data.

artificial intelligence.note: Uncountable — no *a/an* and no plural. It is usually shortened to **AI**: *an AI tool*, *AI is changing schools*. Say the two letters: /ˌeɪ ˈaɪ/.

senses.en: to make a machine or computer do a job that people used to do
examples: The factory has **automated** most of its packing work.
We can **automate** the watering of the school garden.
Many boring office tasks are now **automated**.

forms.en: the use of machines to do work instead of people
forms.ex: **Automation** has changed the way cars are built.

forms.en: working by itself without a person controlling it
forms.ex: The lights in the corridor are **automatic**.

automate.note: **Automatic** describes a thing; **automatically** describes how something happens: *The door opens **automatically***.

senses.en: a way of studying in which you learn a very small amount at a time, usually in lessons of a few minutes
senses.vi: học siêu ngắn (học theo từng đoạn rất ngắn)
examples: **Nanolearning** is popular with students who are always busy.
With **nanolearning**, five minutes on the bus is enough for one lesson.
Our app uses **nanolearning** to teach ten new words a week.

nanolearning.note: A very new word, so many dictionaries do not have it yet. *Nano-* means *extremely small*, so **nanolearning** means learning in very short bursts — often two to five minutes on a phone. Compare *microlearning*, which means almost the same thing.

senses.en: doing a job well without wasting time, money or energy
examples: Electric trains are more **efficient** than old diesel ones.
This robot is **efficient**: it does in one hour what took us a day.
We need a more **efficient** way to sort the rubbish.

forms.en: the quality of working well without waste
forms.ex: The new engine improved the car's **efficiency**.

forms.en: in a way that does not waste time or energy
forms.ex: The team worked quickly and **efficiently**.

efficient.note: **Efficient** = no waste of time or energy. *Effective* = it gives the result you want. A method can be *effective* but not **efficient** if it takes too long.

senses.en: using new ideas or new ways of doing things
examples: The team won the prize for their **innovative** water filter.
Our school has a very **innovative** way of teaching science.
Viet Nam has many **innovative** young start-ups.

forms.en: a new idea or method, or the making of new ideas
forms.ex: This app is the biggest **innovation** in online learning this year.

forms.en: to introduce new ideas or methods
forms.ex: Companies must **innovate** or they will lose customers.

senses.en: an important discovery or change that helps you make progress after a long time
examples: Scientists have made a **breakthrough** in the treatment of malaria.
The new battery is a real **breakthrough** for electric cars.
After months of failure, they finally had a **breakthrough**.

breakthrough.note: The noun is one word, **breakthrough**; the verb phrase is two words: *break through*. We usually say **make** a breakthrough, not ~~do~~ a breakthrough.

senses.en: a room or building where scientists do tests and research
examples: The samples were sent to a **laboratory** for testing.
You must wear glasses and gloves in the **laboratory**.
Our school built a new computer **laboratory** last year.

laboratory.note: The short, everyday form is **lab**: *the school lab*, *lab coat*. Stress differs: British *la-**BOR**-a-try*, American ***LAB**-ra-tory*.

senses.en: a scientific test done to find out what happens or to prove an idea
examples: We did an **experiment** with salt and ice in class today.
The **experiment** showed that the plants grew faster in blue light.
Her first **experiment** failed, so she tried again.

senses.en: to try new things or do scientific tests to see what happens
examples: The class **experimented** with different kinds of soil.
Scientists are **experimenting** with a new kind of plastic.
I like to **experiment** with recipes at the weekend.

forms.en: connected with tests, or still being tested
forms.ex: The hospital is using an **experimental** drug.

experiment.note: The noun and the verb are spelt the same but stressed differently in careful speech, and we say **do** or **carry out** an experiment — not ~~make an experiment~~.

senses.en: to take the place of somebody or something else
examples: Will robots **replace** teachers in the future?
Email has largely **replaced** letters.
Nothing can **replace** a good night's sleep.

senses.en: to put a new or different thing in the position of an old one
examples: We had to **replace** the broken screen.
The school **replaced** all the old lights with LED ones.

senses.en: to put something back where it was before
examples: Please **replace** the books on the shelf when you finish.
He **replaced** the lid carefully so nothing spilled.

replace.note: Say **replace** A **with** B (*We replaced the old PC with a laptop*), or *A was replaced **by** B*. Do not say ~~replace A by a new one~~ in the active voice.

senses.en: a good effect or advantage that something brings
examples: One **benefit** of online learning is that you can study anywhere.
The **benefits** of exercise are well known.
New technology brings both **benefits** and problems.

senses.en: to be helped by something, or to help somebody
senses.vi: hưởng lợi; mang lại lợi ích cho
examples: Farmers **benefit** from weather apps on their phones.
The whole village **benefited** from the new solar panels.
Clean water **benefits** everyone.

forms.en: having a good effect
forms.ex: Reading before bed is **beneficial** for sleep.

benefit.note: The opposite is **drawback** or *disadvantage*. Note the spelling of the verb forms: **benefited**, **benefiting** (one *t* in British and American English).

senses.en: a bad point or problem that makes something less good
examples: The main **drawback** of the robot is its high price.
Studying online has one big **drawback**: you miss your friends.
Every new invention has some **drawbacks**.

drawback.note: **Drawback** is the opposite of **benefit** / *advantage*. It is countable, and it is often used in the pattern *The (main) drawback of X is that…*

senses.en: a program written for a phone or computer to do one particular job
examples: I downloaded an **application** that tests me on ten new words a day.
This **application** turns your handwriting into typed text.
Our maths teacher has built a small **application** for practising fractions.

senses.en: a practical use that a piece of science or technology is put to
senses.vi: sự ứng dụng, việc áp dụng
examples: Eye-tracking has a surprising **application** in the classroom.
The **application** of biometrics to school gates began about ten years ago.
colloc: the application of something to something

senses.en: a formal written request for a place, a job or permission
examples: She sent an **application** to the science summer school in Hue.
My **application** for a library card was accepted the same afternoon.

forms.en: to use something for a purpose, or to make a formal request
forms.ex: Scientists **apply** the same test to every sample.

forms.en: the short everyday word for a phone or computer application
forms.ex: There is an **app** for booking a badminton court.

application.note: In everyday speech nobody says the long word for a phone program — say **app**. Keep **application** for writing, for the *use of a technology* meaning, and for the *form you fill in* meaning.

senses.en: a system or website that people use online to do something together, such as learn, meet or share work
examples: Our school has put every subject on the same **platform**.
Which **platform** does your class use for online lessons?
The **platform** records the lesson so you can watch it again.

senses.en: the raised part of a railway station where you stand to get on a train
examples: The train to Hue leaves from **platform** four.
We waited on a cold **platform** for forty minutes.

senses.en: a flat surface built higher than the floor for somebody to stand on
examples: The speaker climbed onto a small wooden **platform**.
They built a **platform** in the yard for the science fair.

platform.note: Say lessons are **on** a platform, not ~~in~~ a platform: *We study **on** Google Meet.* The name of the platform is capitalised; the word **platform** itself is not.

senses.en: to work on something that already exists over a period of time until it is good enough to use
examples: Engineers spent nine years **developing** this battery before it was safe to sell.
The company is **developing** a cheaper fingerprint scanner for schools.
It takes years to **develop** a technology that ordinary people can afford.

senses.en: to make a skill or a quality of yours stronger by using it
examples: Reading every night **develops** your vocabulary faster than any app.
Group work **develops** the habit of listening before you answer.

senses.en: to grow bigger, stronger or more advanced
examples: The town has **developed** quickly since the new road opened.
A small idea can **develop** into a real invention.

forms.en: the process of growing or of making something better over time
forms.ex: The **development** of the vaccine took eleven months.

forms.en: a person or company that builds software or land
forms.ex: The **developer** fixed the bug in a day.

forms.en: advanced, with modern industry and services
forms.ex: Robot teachers appeared first in **developed** countries.

develop.note: Keep the four apart. You **invent** what never existed, you **discover** what was already there, you **create** something you make yourself, and you **develop** something that exists until it works properly: *Bell **invented** the telephone, and engineers have been **developing** it ever since.* Spelling: one *p* — **developing**, **developed**, never ~~developping~~.

senses.en: using information stored as numbers in a computer, rather than on paper, film or tape
examples: The library is now completely **digital** — there is not one paper card left.
**Digital** communication means we can send a report to Ha Noi in a second.
She keeps a **digital** copy of every experiment she has done.

senses.en: showing information as numbers rather than with hands on a dial
senses.vi: hiển thị số (đồng hồ, nhiệt kế…)
examples: My grandfather still cannot read a **digital** clock quickly.
The **digital** thermometer beeps when it has finished.

forms.en: by computer, in a digital way
forms.ex: The whole test is marked **digitally**.

forms.en: any of the numbers from 0 to 9
forms.ex: A phone number in Viet Nam usually has ten **digits**.

digital.note: The opposite is *analogue*, and for books and letters we usually just say *paper*: *a paper diary* rather than a **digital** one. Note the stress on the first syllable: **DIG**-i-tal.

senses.en: technology that follows where a person's eyes are looking and for how long
senses.vi: công nghệ theo dõi cử động mắt
examples: **Eye-tracking** can show which line of the page a reader stopped at.
Teachers use **eye-tracking** to see whether a class has understood a diagram.
**Eye-tracking** was first used to study how people read, not how they learn.

eye-tracking.note: Written with a hyphen when it sits in front of a noun: *an **eye-tracking** application*. It tells you **where** somebody looked, not what they were thinking — so it is evidence about attention, not about understanding.

senses.en: the fact of being present at school, at a class or at an event
senses.vi: sự có mặt, việc đi học đầy đủ
examples: The school uses a fingerprint scanner to check **attendance** every morning.
Her **attendance** has been perfect since September.
Poor **attendance** is usually the first sign that something is wrong.

senses.en: the number of people who come to an event
examples: The **attendance** at the science fair was over four hundred.
Rain always cuts the **attendance** at our Saturday club.

forms.en: to go to an event, a class or a school
forms.ex: About sixty students **attend** the coding club.

forms.en: a person whose job is to help people in a public place
forms.ex: The car park **attendant** showed us where to wait.

attendance.note: In a school the fixed phrase is **check attendance** or **take attendance** — the moment the teacher finds out who is absent. Note the spelling: *-ance*, not ~~attendence~~.

senses.en: the act of staying away from school without permission
examples: Biometrics is meant to put an end to **truancy** and to copying in tests.
**Truancy** fell sharply once parents got a message the moment a class began.
The head teacher treats **truancy** as a problem to solve, not only to punish.

forms.en: a student who stays away from school without permission
forms.ex: Two **truants** were found at the market.

forms.en: to stay away from school without permission
forms.ex: He **played truant** twice and regretted it.

truancy.note: **Truancy** is the behaviour and it is uncountable — never ~~a truancy~~, ~~truancies~~. It always means *without permission*: a day off for a dentist's appointment is not **truancy**.

senses.en: the act of breaking the rules of a test or a game in order to gain an advantage
examples: The new system was bought to stop **cheating** in end-of-term tests.
**Cheating** in an online exam is harder than students think.
Copying one line of a friend's homework is still **cheating**.

forms.en: to break the rules of a test or game in order to win or pass
forms.ex: Nobody **cheats** when the questions are all different.

forms.en: a person who breaks the rules to win
forms.ex: No one wants to play cards with a **cheat**.

cheating.note: You **cheat in** a test or an exam, and you **cheat at** a game: *cheat **in** the maths test*, *cheat **at** chess*. **Cheating** is uncountable — never ~~a cheating~~.

senses.en: what somebody tells you about your work, so that you know what to keep and what to change
senses.vi: ý kiến phản hồi, nhận xét
examples: The teacher marks my work and sends **feedback** the next morning.
Her **feedback** was short: two good sentences and one thing to fix.
A robot can give **feedback** on spelling, but not on an idea.

senses.en: opinions that users give about a product or a service
examples: The app changed its colours after **feedback** from teachers.
We collected **feedback** from every class before choosing a platform.

feedback.note: Uncountable: **feedback**, never ~~a feedback~~ or ~~feedbacks~~. If you need to count, say *a piece of **feedback*** or *some comments*. Use **on**: *feedback **on** my essay*.

senses.en: a small separate space in an online class where a few students go to work together
senses.vi: phòng thảo luận nhóm trực tuyến
examples: Our teacher puts us into **breakout rooms** so that four of us can discuss one question.
In the **breakout room** we argued about the answer for ten minutes.
She visits every **breakout room** once and then calls us all back.

breakout room.note: Two words, and usually plural because a class is split into several: *into **breakout rooms***. The teacher **puts** or **sends** students **into** them, and the students **go into** or **join** one.

senses.en: with the other person really there in the room, not on a screen or a phone
examples: I would rather meet my classmates **face to face** than in twenty small squares.
We had emailed for a year before we finally met **face to face**.
Some things are easier to say **face to face**.

senses.grammar: before a noun, usually written face-to-face
senses.en: happening with people together in the same place
examples: Ann prefers **face-to-face** classes because she likes talking to her friends.
Our club runs one online meeting and one **face-to-face** meeting a month.

face to face.note: Three separate words after the verb (*we met **face to face***), but hyphenated in front of a noun (*a **face-to-face** class*). The opposite in a school is *online* or *remote*.

senses.en: to say that you are not happy about something, or that something is wrong
examples: Half the class **complain** about the Internet connection every single week.
He **complained** that the robot never explained anything twice.
Nobody **complains** when the lesson finishes early.

senses.en: to tell somebody in charge, formally, that something is wrong
examples: My father **complained** to the school about the broken projector.
If the app charges you twice, **complain** at once.

forms.en: a statement that something is wrong or unsatisfactory
forms.vi: lời phàn nàn, đơn khiếu nại
forms.ex: The commonest **complaint** was about the noise.

complain.note: **Complain about** a thing, **complain to** a person: *She **complained to** the teacher **about** the noise.* Never ~~complain something~~. The noun changes its ending: **complaint**, not ~~complainment~~.

senses.en: a disease that spreads quickly through a lot of people in one area at the same time
examples: My class moved onto Zoom during the **epidemic** and never fully moved back.
The village closed its market for a month during the **epidemic**.
Clean water stopped the **epidemic** faster than any medicine.

forms.en: spreading very quickly among many people
forms.ex: The illness became **epidemic** within three weeks.

epidemic.note: An **epidemic** is in one country or area; a *pandemic* has spread across the world. Stress the third syllable: ep-i-**DEM**-ic.

senses.en: a small round piece of thin plastic that you wear on your eye to help you see clearly
examples: My aunt wears **contact lenses** instead of glasses when she plays badminton.
One **contact lens** fell out during the experiment.
Scientists say a 3D **contact lens** will one day show a whole film.

contact lens.note: Plural **contact lenses**, with *-es*. You **wear** them and you **put** them **in**; you do not ~~use~~ them. Two words in British English, and the everyday short form is just *contacts*.

senses.en: to repair something that is broken or torn, so that it works or can be used again
examples: He **mends** boat engines all day.
She **mended** the net before the tide turned.
Can you **mend** it, or do we need a new one?

mend.note: **Mend** and **repair** are the same act; *mend* is the everyday word and is what you use for small things — a net, a shirt, a lock. **Fix** works for all of them and is the commonest of the three in speech.
